newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close lower, 5-year note sale weak.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close lower, 5-year note sale weak.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower in thin trade, dragged down by weak results in the Treasury's monthly auction of fresh five-year notes, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 3/32 at 97-3/32. Its yield rose to 6.98 percent, but failed to touch a 7.0 percent technical resistance barrier.

The Treasury faced some difficulty to sell $12.5 billion of five-year notes as players remained wary of buying new securities at a time when the specter of a possible Federal Reserve tightening continued to haunt the market.

The notes were placed with a yield of 6.568 percent, above the 6.555 percent forecasts. The bid-to-cover ratio was at a low 2.13, showing demand for the issues was slack. Non- competitive bids were at $534 million.

Wall Street dealers were seen as being responsible for most of the underwriting of the new issues. No broad-based retail buying was seen. Some mild foreign interest, mainly from Asian investors, was detected.
But pundits said foreigners were not as active in Wednesday's auction as they were in the Treasury's two-year note sale on Tuesday.

"The bid-to-cover ratio was on the low side ... and there wasn't much customer participation," said John Spinello, managing director of government securities at Merrill Lynch Government Securities Inc.
"I think the dealers (were) short enough to have an underwriting bid," Spinello added.
Analysts said some professional selling in the futures market at the Chicago Board of Trade shortly after the auction deadline at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT also weighed on prices.
The weakness registered in the Treasury's auctions this week may weigh a bit on prices, mainly in a week that is characterized by a soft flow of fresh data.

"I think (the new issues) will be a little bit of a burden ... We didn't have any good broad-based retail underwriting. So a lot of this is probably still in the Street hands and it's going to be distributed over time," Spinello said.

Still, analysts will keep their eyes open to new jobless claims data and a revision for the second quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) numbers on Thursday as well as the August Chicago Purchasing Managers index on Friday.

"That's what we'll be chewing until we get to the August payrolls," said a trader at a foreign bank. The August employment report, due out on September 6, is seen as key to help the market set its short-term direction.
The indicator is also seen as a crucial report to be used by the Fed during the September 24 meeting of its policy- setting arm, the Federal Open Market Committee.
Although there is no consensus yet, analysts said sentiment the Fed could tighten monetary policy in September was growing in the aisles of Wall Street buildings.
"The market is 50/50 on September," said Patrick Dimick, economist at CS First Boston, referring to the possibility of a Fed tightening next month.
"And what that means is that we're going to have a lot of volatility in the front end of the yield curve ... Right now, every little bit of information matters," Dimick added.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up one basis point at 5.06 percent. The six-month bill was flat at 5.14 percent. The year bill closed down unchanged at 5.44 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 99-29/32, yielding 6.18 percent. The five-year note traded off 1/32 at 100-9/32 to yield 6.56 percent. The ten-year note fell 2/32 at 101-16/32, yielding 6.79 percent.
